final_recommendation: The room converged on a protocol amendment with a 15-day joint commission review, automatic tariff suspension on day 16 if no consensus, and Mexico's inspection documentation deemed sufficient unless the U.S. provides concrete proof of non-compliance. Congress committed to a Q1 floor vote contingent on Friday EOB protocol text locking this language, with all parties explicitly agreeing no other chapters would be reopened.
minority_objections: Labor union initially demanded day-61 automatic suspension with no dispute resolution window, which was rejected in favor of the 15-day commission process
Congressional Democrats initially sought unilateral U.S. suspension authority, which was denied as contradicting the joint-commission framework
key_conflicts: Mexico's sovereignty concern versus U.S. labor enforcement demands: resolved by defining 'concrete evidence' as inspection-timeline gaps verified by Mexico's own records, shifting burden of proof to U.S.
Business lobby's certainty demands versus labor's enforcement mechanism requirements: bridged by the 15-day commission with automatic mechanical suspension
Canada's fear of wholesale renegotiation versus U.S. need to reopen labor enforcement: resolved by explicit commitment that protocol amendment would not touch other chapters
key_concessions: Mexico accepted 60-day inspection timelines with automatic tariff suspension if joint commission deadlocks by day 16
U.S. Congress accepted joint commission process instead of unilateral suspension authority
Labor unions accepted 15-day commission review window instead of immediate day-61 suspension
All parties accepted 'Mexico's documentation sufficient unless U.S. provides concrete proof' burden-shift language
red_lines: Mexico: no unilateral U.S. suspension without joint commission process and burden of proof on U.S.
U.S. Congress: no floor vote without mechanical enforcement mechanism in writing by Friday EOB
Canada: no reopening of dairy, Chapter 19, or any other settled chapters beyond labor enforcement
Labor unions: no ratification support without automatic suspension language and defined 'concrete evidence' standard
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Implementation capacity: no discussion of whether Mexico's labor inspection infrastructure can actually meet 60-day timelines at scale
Litigation risk: minimal discussion of how 'concrete evidence' standard would be litigated in practice or whether it survives WTO challenge
Political sustainability in Mexico: no discussion of domestic Mexican political backlash to U.S. enforcement mechanism
Business disruption during enforcement: no discussion of supply-chain impacts if tariffs suspend during commission review periods
downstream_risk_variables: Whether Friday EOB protocol text actually locks the agreed 'sufficient unless' language or waters it down to 'both sides present evidence'
Whether Mexico's labor inspection system can operationally deliver 60-day timelines once agreement is in force
Whether the 15-day commission process becomes a recurring source of U.S.-Mexico friction and tariff uncertainty
Whether Canada's explicit 'no other chapters' red line holds if future political pressure emerges to revisit other terms
uncertainty_notes: The room achieved conditional convergence on protocol language, but final ratification depends entirely on whether the Friday EOB text actually locks the agreed 'Mexico's documentation sufficient unless U.S. provides concrete proof' language. If the drafting team waters this down to 'both sides present evidence,' Mexico and labor both indicated they would walk. The Q1 floor vote commitment is explicitly contingent on this language holding. No discussion occurred of operational implementation capacity or long-term enforcement sustainability.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congressman stated 'I've got the votes to kill this thing or move it' and repeatedly conditioned floor vote on Friday protocol text; ratification risk drove the entire negotiation structure and Friday deadline
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Labor enforcement mechanism (60-day inspections, 15-day commission, automatic suspension) was the central, driving issue in every round; unions and Congress made it the condition for ratification support
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Business lobby actively participated and secured Q1 floor vote commitment, but was not the dominant driver—played supporting role to labor enforcement and ratification risk themes
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Canada repeatedly demanded assurance that protocol would not reopen other chapters, but this was defensive/protective rather than driving the room's direction
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Mexico's sovereignty concern (joint commission vs. unilateral U.S. action, burden of proof) was a central, driving constraint that shaped the final 'sufficient unless' language and 15-day commission structure
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Media actor repeatedly framed narrative implications and headline outcomes, influencing urgency and public commitment, but was not the dominant substantive driver
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: The entire room treated agreement stability as contingent on the protocol amendment—no participant argued for ratifying as-is; stability required the enforcement mechanism compromise
